entry.title: A Swipe Labeller for YIMBY and NIMBY Comments
entry.content:
TLDR:

  • I built a phone page for labelling public comments from Bay Area meetings. Friends read and hear each comment and say whether the speaker is a YIMBY or a NIMBY.
  • The answers are a human check on the automated labels in the Exploratory Dashboard of Bay Area Public Meetings.
  • I tried three designs and chose Option C: one YIMBY or NIMBY question, answered with a swipe.

YIMBY means "yes in my backyard": the speaker wants more homes, or more transit, walking or cycling, built in their area. NIMBY means "not in my backyard": the speaker is against it in their area.

Option A: two questions. The labeller picks the topic, then picks for, against or neutral. This records the topic and the stance separately.

Option B: one question, for or against. The labeller swipes right for "for" and left for "against". It takes one action per comment instead of three.

Option C: one question, YIMBY or NIMBY. This is the one I chose. The swipe is the same as in Option B, but the answers are YIMBY and NIMBY. These are the words the study uses, so the answers need no translation before they are compared with the automated labels.

The final version. It is Option C with one change: it asks one general question for housing and transit together, instead of one session for each. The words light up as the audio plays, and a swipe saves the answer and shows the next comment.

entry.title: Dashboard for Twitch Transcripts
entry.content:
TLDR

  • I transcribed HasanAbi's Twitch streams, from the archived video audio, with a speech recognition model.
  • I counted how much of each stream had speech and which words came up most.
  • I found that three Michigan politicians were named most often in the final streams before the midterms.
  • The panels below show hours, topics and words by stream. Methods are at the end.

Show

Words near a word

Or pick a topic

People named

Names were found with spaCy, a language-processing library, which marks the words in a sentence that name a person. Mentions are grouped by surname, so "Stevens" alone counts as Haley Stevens. A first name alone, such as "Abdul", is not counted. The streamer himself, fictional characters and religious figures were left out. Each cell gives how often the person was named per 10,000 words in that stream.

Stream length Speech

Selected topics

Methods. The streams are the HasanAbi Twitch broadcasts transcribed so far, listed in the charts. New streams and older archived streams are added as they are transcribed. On days with many streams, each chart scrolls sideways. Dates are stream start dates in Pacific time. The audio of each archived stream was transcribed in full with WhisperX, using the Whisper large-v3 model. Speech hours are the summed length of the segments where the model wrote text. Words are counted as the model wrote them, split on spaces. The transcripts include every voice on stream: the host, guests, and audio from videos played on stream. Topic and word rates count word tokens, which are runs of letters with an optional apostrophe, per 10,000 tokens in the stream. A possessive counts as its word, so "Israel's" counts as "Israel". The speech recognition spells Abdul El-Sayed several ways, such as "Abdullah Al-Sayed" and "Abdel El-Sayed". All of them count as "Abdul El-Sayed". Each topic is a fixed word list, shown under its chart. The word grid opens on word pairs. A pair is two tokens spoken one after the other in the same segment. Neither token is a common English word, and each has at least three letters. Pairs with the streamer's own name were removed. The single-words view uses the 12 most frequent words over all eight streams after common English words were removed. Spoken filler that the common-word list misses was also removed, for example "thank" and "wait". So were first names whose surname is already counted, and the streamer's own names. Speech recognition makes mistakes, mostly in names and in crosstalk, so counts are approximate. This page shows only counts and rates; no transcript text is published.

References #

HasanAbi. (2026). Twitch past broadcasts, 2026 [Video recordings]. Twitch. https://www.twitch.tv/hasanabi

Bain, M., Huh, J., Han, T., & Zisserman, A. (2023). WhisperX: Time-accurate speech transcription of long-form audio. Proceedings of Interspeech 2023, 4489 to 4493. https://github.com/m-bain/whisperX

Radford, A., Kim, J. W., Xu, T., Brockman, G., McLeavey, C., & Sutskever, I. (2023). Robust speech recognition via large-scale weak supervision. Proceedings of the 40th International Conference on Machine Learning. https://github.com/openai/whisper

Honnibal, M., Montani, I., Van Landeghem, S., & Boyd, A. (2020). spaCy: Industrial-strength natural language processing in Python [Computer software]. https://spacy.io/

entry.title: LA Metro Rail Ridership by Line and Station, 2026
entry.content:
Station boardings in fiscal year 2026, by year opened

Average weekday boardings by line, fiscal years 2009 to 2026

The dashed vertical line marks June 2023, when the Regional Connector tunnel downtown changed the routes of the A and E Lines. Their figures before that line are for the earlier routes. LA Metro reports the B and D Lines as one figure, drawn in red and purple dashes.

Methods. Station places, names and lines come from the LA Metro rail GTFS feed. GTFS is the standard timetable format that transit agencies publish. Opening dates come from the Wikipedia list of LA Metro Rail stations, which cites LA Metro. Line widths and the line chart use average weekday boardings by line, fiscal years 2009 to 2026. They come from LA Metro's Interactive Estimated Ridership Stats, retrieved 29 October 2026. LA Metro reports the B and D Lines together as the B Line, so they share one width. The A and E Lines took their current routes in June 2023, when the Regional Connector opened. Their line data starts in fiscal year 2024, and earlier years draw them thin. The former L Line is not drawn. Fiscal year 2009 covers 127 weekdays. Width grows with the square root of boardings. Station boardings, in the busiest-10 bars and the scatter chart, are average weekday boardings by station for LA Metro fiscal years 2024, 2025 and 2026. A fiscal year runs from July to June and is named for the year it ends. LA Metro released these figures through public records requests, and they were copied from three dated versions of a Wikipedia table that cites those releases. Boardings by station are not available before fiscal year 2024, so the 2020 drop does not show here. Stations that opened during a fiscal year have an average over the days they were open. Lines are drawn with their 2026 names and colors in every year. Expo / Crenshaw has two platforms in the feed and is drawn as one station. In fiscal year 2024, Lynwood was named Long Beach Boulevard. The North Hollywood figure for fiscal years 2025 and 2026 includes G Line bus boardings. The map uses the 2024 county boundary file. A pin marks each station that opened in 2025 or 2026. Contour lines are drawn every 100 m of elevation, with every 500 m line darker. They were built from AWS Terrain Tiles at zoom 10, about 130 m per cell, smoothed and simplified.

entry.title: Gathering Drug Target Evidence With a Model That Only Paraphrases
entry.content:
TLDR:

  • I set out to make a demo that aggregates the top genetic targets for a disease into one figure, to motivate biologists to take those genes into early in vitro target validation experiments.
  • I built a tool that turns a disease name into that figure: for each differentially expressed gene, its druggability, safety, tissue expression, drug pipeline, literature and mouse phenotypes.
  • I added a language model that writes one short evidence paragraph per gene from the gathered facts only, stored with the run, and never ranks, filters or decides anything.
  • The tool and the code are public.

targetring takes a disease, finds a public gene expression study for it, picks a comparison of affected against unaffected people, and draws a ring figure for the genes that differ. Each ring is one source: tractability and safety from Open Targets, tissue expression from GTEx, development level from Pharos, mechanisms from ChEMBL, literature counts from Europe PMC and PubTator, mouse phenotypes from MGI. A missing cell is drawn as missing, never as zero, because the figure used to be built by hand from six browser tabs and the hardest part was knowing whether an empty cell meant "not measured" or "the lookup failed". Clicking a gene opens a drawer with the full drug pipeline, the trials behind it, and a GO or NO-GO line from a fixed three part rule: expressed in a disease tissue, dysregulated in the study, and a phenotype on record.

The language model's job is deliberately small, and the prompt is where that is enforced. For each gene the tool assembles the facts it already fetched and sends them once to a model whose only permitted source is that JSON: nothing it knows about the gene, the disease or the drugs may enter the text, and a fact that is not in the JSON does not exist. The prompt fixes the paragraph's length at four to six sentences and its order sentence by sentence: the rule-based verdict restated word for word, then the hypothesis the fold change implies, then the evidence that is present, then every ring with no data named as absent rather than low. It bans recommendations, rankings against other genes, invented citations, hedging phrases, em dashes, percentages, internal codes and identifiers, and gives the plain gloss to use for each code. The other three model calls in the tool are constrained the same way: each chooses only from a closed list the app supplied, the answer is checked against that list on return, and when a call fails the rule-based fallback runs and the figure records who chose. The paragraph is then stored with the run. The same facts always produce the same stored paragraph, so the four demo runs needed 13 calls for 46 genes, and the whole demo's model spend was $1.35, measured 18 October 2026 and shown on the tool's Paid calls tab. A second, smaller call reads the gene's mouse phenotype terms against the disease area and returns a 0 or 1, printed beside the rule-based phenotype check and never replacing it. The drawer below shows that line for MUC1 in the Crohn's run. The stored paragraph for the same gene begins with the verdict and its three reasons, then the fold change, the tissue expression against the median across 54 tissues, the mouse phenotypes, and the empty drug pipeline, each with its number and unit, and no opinion of its own.

entry.title: A Queue Model of an Emergency Department, to Size an Intervention
entry.content:
TLDR:

  • I had assumed a treatment effect in an earlier decision analysis, and could not say whether the number was modest or absurd.
  • I read how emergency departments are usually simulated, then built a discrete-event model of a boarding queue and tuned it until its morning trolley count tracked one real hospital.
  • Found that the queue is the overflow from a small shortfall in beds, which makes every intervention I tested larger than the problem it is aimed at.
  • The executed notebook, the model code and the figures are on GitHub.

Earlier this month I added a decision analysis to my trolley forecast. The weakest part of it was the treatment effect. I had assumed a patient flow intervention would cut the growth in pressure by 15 of 100, and the whole recommendation depended on that number. A forecast cannot say whether the number is plausible, so I built a model of the process that produces the trolley count.

Discrete-event simulation is the standard tool for this. I followed the Little Book of DES, a free guide to building health service simulations in SimPy, for the model structure: patients arrive at a time varying rate, compete for resources, and the model runs through a warm-up period before anything is recorded.

The model is written in SimPy. Patients arrive on a Poisson process whose rate varies by hour and by day of week, wait for an assessment space, and a share of them are admitted. Admitted patients join a first in, first out queue for an inpatient bed. The length of that queue at 8 am is the trolley count, that is the number of admitted patients waiting on trolleys, or gurneys, for a bed. Beds are released in discharge windows that cluster in the late morning and thin out at the weekend, which is why the queue is longest first thing and shortest on a Saturday.

I calibrated it to University Hospital Limerick, which has a complete daily record since January 2023 and the largest counts in the series. Two inputs came from data. The bed count is in my own supplementary data: 553 open inpatient beds in 2025. The daily report also records surge capacity in use, the extra spaces a hospital opens under pressure, and at this hospital that rises with the trolley count. I fitted that relationship and used it as the model's escalation rule. Without it the ward runs at full occupancy, the queue has no stable average, and the simulated count drifts for months at a time.

Everything else is assumed and tuned: the arrival rate, the share admitted, the average stay. I searched a grid of 108 combinations, scoring each on how closely its day of week averages matched the real ones. The best set reproduces the window average, 39 trolleys against 40 observed, and on the eight weeks I held back it is wrong by 12.7 trolleys on an average day. In the plot above the simulated average is the flat blue line. What it misses is the swing from month to month, from about 22 trolleys in November 2025 to about 56 in January 2026.

The grid also shows the limit of the method. Ten of the 108 combinations fit within 1 trolley per day of the best one, because a single observed count cannot separate the arrival rate from the admission share from the length of stay. What it does identify is the gap between the bed days emergency admissions demand and the beds available to meet them. Every well fitting combination is between 2 and 14 beds short.

Then the three scenarios, each run 60 times with different seeds. Opening 20 more beds takes the average morning count from 39 trolleys to 13, with a likely range of 9 to 17. Half a day off the average stay brings it to 3, likely range 2 to 5. Removing 15 of 100 admitted patients from the queue, the effect I assumed in the decision analysis, brings it to roughly zero. The high days also disappear. The hospital went above 56 trolleys on one day in four over the window. In the scenarios that falls to 2 days in 100 or fewer.

The panels above vary one lever at a time, and in each the curve is steep at the left and flat at the right. That is the answer I wanted, and it shows that my assumption was too large. Half a day off a six day stay frees about as many bed days as 39 beds, and removing 15 of 100 admissions frees about as many as 70. Against a shortfall of 8 beds all three are far larger than the problem. An intervention that genuinely delivered a 15 of 100 reduction would not cut pressure at this hospital by 15 of 100. It would end boarding. Against a January level baseline, where the shortfall is larger, the ordering held: 20 beds leave 20 trolleys behind rather than 13.

What this is: a demonstration that a queue model fitted to one real series answers a question a forecast cannot, which is how large a change has to be before it moves anything. What it is not: a description of how University Hospital Limerick works, a forecast, or evidence about any intervention. The notebook keeps what was observed apart from what was assumed, so each input can be checked. The executed notebook and the model module are on GitHub.

entry.title: Learning Decision Analysis on Top of a Hospital Forecast
entry.content:
TLDR:

  • I wanted to learn what decision analysis adds to a forecast, so I put a small decision model on top of the trolley forecast from my thesis.
  • I read two books on decision analysis and built the smallest version of the idea: one region, one week, one yes or no choice.
  • Found that the forecast alone never said what to do. The answer came from three assumptions I had to write down, and the model showed where each one changed it.
  • The executed notebook, design notes and figures are on GitHub.

My trolley post ended with a forecast of how many admitted patients would be waiting on trolleys for a hospital bed. A forecast does not tell a manager whether to act on it. This post adds that step. The question is simple: should a hospital switch on an extra patient flow intervention before a forecast spike? The hospital data are real. The spike, the effect of the intervention and its cost are made up, because the point was to learn the method.

The model has four parts. A forecast for one week in one region, HSE Dublin and Midlands, with its spread of plausible values. A made up spike added to it. An assumed effect of the intervention, a cut of 15 of 100 in the growth above the current rate, with its own spread. And a penalty for acting, written on the same scale as the trolley rate. The rule is to pick the choice with the lower expected loss, where the loss is the trolley rate left over plus the penalty.

With the spike, the forecast was 5.48 trolleys per 10,000 residents, likely range 5.26 to 5.69. Intervening cut the expected loss from 5.48 to 5.15 after the penalty, and beat doing nothing in 92 of 100 scenarios drawn from the model. The most useful number was the break even penalty, 0.35 per 10,000: below that cost the model intervenes, above it the model does not. That turns "should we act" into "is acting cheaper than this", which someone who knows the hospital can answer.

Changing one input at a time showed where the answer flips. A spike too small to cross the pressure cutoff means no intervention is considered. A zero average effect means doing nothing wins. A penalty of 0.40 means doing nothing wins. Doubling the spread of the effect kept the same average answer but cut the winning share from 92 of 100 to 76 of 100. The recommendation was never a property of the forecast. It was the forecast plus three assumptions, and the model let me change each one and see when the answer changed.

This is a learning exercise, not evidence that the intervention reduces crowding or saves money. The books were Smart Choices and Bayesian Decision Analysis. The executed notebook has every number.

entry.title: HSE Mid West had significantly more patients on trolleys than any other region, 8.1 per 10,000 people a week
entry.content:
HSE Mid West had a level of 8.1 patients on trolleys per 10,000 people a week (95% credible interval 7.4 to 8.8). That is 1.6 more than HSE West and North West, the next highest (95% credible interval 0.7 to 2.5 more). Every region dropped in the week that contains 25 December. The drop ran from 2.3 per 10,000 in HSE Dublin and North East to 5.4 per 10,000 in HSE Mid West.

The four New Year phases, weeks starting Monday
PhaseWeeks

Methods. Data are daily counts of patients on emergency department and ward trolleys from the HSE Urgent and Emergency Care daily report, 1 January 2023 to 5 April 2026, summed into Monday-start weeks for each region and divided by regional population per 10,000 people. The estimates come from model v4.6 of Henry and Bergin (2026): each region has its own level, a yearly cycle, four New Year phase effects, a Mid West operational reset in August 2024, and dependence on the previous two weeks. It was fitted in JAGS with 4 chains of 30,000 iterations, the first 10,000 dropped, giving 80,000 draws. Values are posterior medians. The 95% credible interval runs from the 2.5th to the 97.5th percentile of the draws. Significantly means the 95% credible interval of a difference between two regions excludes zero. A probability is the share of the 80,000 draws in which the statement holds. The seasonal swing is how far the yearly cycle rises above the level at its peak. Winter follows Met Éireann (2026) and the thesis: 1 December to the end of February. The winter excess is the region's yearly cycle averaged over study weeks starting in December to February, minus its average over the other study weeks, computed in every draw. It uses the yearly cycle only, not the New Year phases. The four phases are the week two weeks before the week containing 1 January, the week before it, which contains 25 December, the week containing 1 January, and the week after it. Each phase effect is the change from the baseline average in that week, and the same effect applies every winter. The yearly peak is the date where the fitted yearly cycle is highest, found in each draw from its sine and cosine terms. The probability of a winter peak is the share of draws with that date from 1 December to the end of February. The peak's 95% credible interval is the shortest stretch of the calendar that holds 95% of the draws. Region boundaries were simplified for display.

References #

Henry, L., & Bergin, E. (2026). A Bayesian time series framework for comparing on trolley counts across Irish HSE health regions [Master's thesis, University of Galway].

Henry, L., & Bergin, E. (2026). HSE urgent care report Bayesian analysis [Computer software]. GitHub. https://github.com/hotsoupisgood/hse-urgent-care-report-trolley-analysis

Health Service Executive. (2026). Urgent and emergency care report [Data set]. https://www2.hse.ie/services/urgent-emergency-care-report/

Met Éireann. (2026). Climate of Ireland. The Irish Meteorological Service. https://www.met.ie/climate/climate-of-ireland

Bostock, M. (2023). D3.js (Version 7) [Computer software]. https://d3js.org/

entry.title: How I Learn With LLMs
entry.content:
TLDR:

  • I made a flowchart of how I usually learn things with LLMs.

Studying with LLMs has taken some getting used to, but I have settled into a pattern when I use them to learn or build something technical. The flowchart below has the steps I roughly follow. I almost always begin with Wikipedia. The first couple of paragraphs are usually a good initial summary. Then I hit some friction, usually because Wikipedia is not always written in a gentle way. At that point I go to the best LLM at the time and ask it for the best sources on the subject. For something biological or novel I ask for a scientific review. For something more technical or standard I ask for textbook recommendations. I find these types of sources make the best learning paths.

I then work through the source, asking an LLM for help when needed, either for worked examples or to fill gaps. If a source does not work out, I move on to another one. I am a visual person and the gif below shows how I think about this loop. You fill in the gaps with back and forths. This works even better with an actual subject matter expert instead of an LLM, but that is rarely possible. Once I am satisfied with my understanding I put all my notes together and do a final write up. That could be a presentation, a digital document, or pen and paper.

Everyone does this a little differently, but this is what works best for me so far.

entry.title: Do LLMs Frame the Same Chart Differently?
entry.content:
TLDR:

  • I asked three LLMs to interpret four controversial plots 250 times each, then compared the sentiment of their responses.
  • Most comparisons were significantly different. Grok was the usual outlier, lowest on the climate and COVID plots and highest on the pay gap plot.
  • The differences seem to come down to word choice. Auditing a handful of Grok responses did not show an obvious polarized opinion, but in the word drivers plot Grok's word choices looked the most different from the other two. All of this can be seen in the dashboard.

In the zeitgeist of the internet there are memes about Grok being anti woke and hyperbolic, and it has recited climate denial talking points, brought up South African "white genocide" in unrelated replies, and posted antisemitic content. If that's real, it should read certain plots differently from other models. So my hypothesis was that Grok's interpretations of a race and IQ plot, a climate plot, a COVID deaths and masks plot, and a gender pay gap plot would lean racist, anti climate change, critical of COVID related government actions, and dismissive of the pay gap, and that this would show up as more negative sentiment on all four. All four were picked to be potentially misleading, with political connotations. The prompt was the same every time, "Interpret this plot."

Power calculation. Running LLMs on images is relatively expensive, so I wanted to know how many replies I actually needed before spending anything. Earlier runs with the previous model generation had an SD of 0.39 in sentiment within a model and plot pair. To detect a 0.10 difference between two models at 80% power, with a small penalty for using a rank test, that gives about 250 replies per model per plot.

Pilot. A pilot of 50 per cell with the current models, Claude Opus 5, GPT-5.5 and Grok 4.7, came out at SD 0.52. They write longer and more varied replies than the last generation. Detecting 0.10, after correcting for three comparisons per plot, would now need about 600 per cell. I kept n at 250, which means the smallest detectable difference is about 0.15, and froze that before collecting any more data. Changing n after seeing p values is optional stopping, so I also removed a "show to panel and loop back" step from the plan and kept the old version for the record.

Scoring. Each of the 3,000 replies was scored with VADER, which gives a sentiment from −1 to +1. VADER scores based on a corpus of rated words, not a model, which matters below.

Tests. For each plot, three pairwise Mann-Whitney U tests, Bonferroni corrected, with Cliff's delta and a bootstrap 95% CI on the mean difference.

Chart Claude ChatGPT Grok
CO2 / climate +0.65 +0.63 +0.36
COVID & masks +0.24 +0.09 −0.34
Gender pay gap +0.28 +0.24 +0.69
Race & IQ +0.32 −0.12 +0.18

Results. 11 of 12 pairwise comparisons are significant. Grok has the lowest sentiment on climate and COVID and the highest on the pay gap. On race and IQ it sits in the middle, and ChatGPT is the only model that goes negative.

Which words drove it. On the climate plot the top positive words are "warming", "perfectly" and "increase", and the top negative word is "misleading". "Perfectly" is almost always "perfectly flat" and "misleading" is about the axis, so neither is about climate at all, and VADER rates "warming" and "increase" as pleasant words, which they aren't here. All three models say the same thing about that plot, that the wide axis hides a real rise, and Claude says "misleading" in 244 of its 250 replies yet scores highest because its long replies pick up more positive words. Grok's low score comes from shorter replies with fewer of those words, not from a different view of climate change.

So the differences between models are real, but the sentiment is misleading once you look at the words behind it. VADER measured vocabulary and reply length, not stance, and the hypothesis about Grok is neither supported nor refuted by it. Every reply is readable on the results page, and the code is on GitHub.

A future direction would be to use a human or an LLM as a judge to rate whether each reply treats the pay gap as real, which would test the original hypothesis directly.

entry.title: Exploratory Dashboard of Bay Area Public Meetings
entry.content:
A YIMBY ("yes in my backyard") speaker supports more housing or transit being built. A NIMBY ("not in my backyard") speaker opposes it, often near where they live. Each bar shows how many more of a body's speakers were coded YIMBY than NIMBY, of every 100 with a stance.

Show
Body

The grid shows the 12 most frequent single words in the coded meeting stretches, after common English words were removed. Words about running the meeting, such as "council" and "mayor", place names, such as "Clara" and "Napa", and spoken filler, such as "questions" and "people", were also removed. Each cell gives how often the word was said per 10,000 words in that month. Bodies with fewer than 30,000 transcribed words have no tab of their own but count in All.

The grid shows the 12 most frequent 3-word phrases in the coded meeting stretches. A phrase counts once per speaker per meeting stretch, so one person repeating a line adds one. The first and last words are not common English words. Phrases about running the meeting, such as calls to speak and votes, place names, the Pledge of Allegiance and phrases with a person's given name were removed. Each cell gives how often the phrase was said per 10,000 words in that month.

The grid shows the 12 most frequent 4-word phrases in the coded meeting stretches. A phrase counts once per speaker per meeting stretch, so one person repeating a line adds one. The first and last words are not common English words. Phrases about running the meeting, such as calls to speak and votes, place names, the Pledge of Allegiance and phrases with a person's given name were removed. Each cell gives how often the phrase was said per 10,000 words in that month.

The grid shows the 12 most frequent word pairs in the coded meeting stretches. A word pair is two words said one after the other, neither of them a common English word. Pairs about running the meeting, such as "council member" and "public comment", and place names, such as "San Jose", were removed. Each cell gives how often the pair was said per 10,000 words in that month. Bodies with fewer than 30,000 transcribed words have no tab of their own but count in All.

Or pick a word
Nearby words

Positive wordNegative word

Methods. Word pairs and phrases are counted in the published, redacted transcripts; a redaction mark breaks a phrase. One public commenter opens and closes with the same two lines at many BART and VTA meetings; those lines are removed before counting. A speaker is one voice at one stretch of a meeting. Each statement was scored from -2, opposing more housing or transit, to +2, supporting more of it. A speaker is YIMBY when their statements average +0.5 or higher and NIMBY at -0.5 or lower. The likely range is a 90 in 100 interval from 2,000 resamples of meeting stretches. Significant means the result passes a test corrected for checking many bodies at once. The correction is the Holm method, applied to the 15 public-speaker results and, separately, to the 24 official results, at 10 in 100. A likely range that excludes zero is not enough on its own. A body is drawn when it has at least 10 speakers with a stance in that group. Faint lines on the map are elevation contours every 150 meters, from the Terrain Tiles data set. Transit boards are placed at their headquarters city and the county board at the county's center. Exploratory analysis. Stance and tone were coded by a large language model and have not been validated against human coders. All figures are copied from the project's published data of 2026-10-25.

entry.title: Cappuccino Index Claim Significance
entry.content:
TLDR:

  • Hoffmann's cappuccino index puts Italy second, just behind Australia.
  • That ranking rests on about 15 survey responses from Italy.
  • With that little data, Italy isn't significantly different from eleven other countries, including first place Australia.

James Hoffmann's new video on the cappuccino index surveys baristas for the country they work in, the price of a cappuccino at their café, and their hourly wage, then uses the number of cappuccinos a barista could buy with an hour's wage to rank countries. By his numbers, Italy comes in second overall, just behind Australia. The problem is the survey is small and self-selected, so I wanted to know whether that gap between countries is real or just noise.

I focused on Italy and Australia since James called them out directly. So I bootstrapped the samples and plotted the mean and 95% confidence interval for every country, shown below.

Italy stands out immediately. It has the widest confidence interval of any country, and its true mean ratio could plausibly sit anywhere from about 3.6 to 8.4. That's too wide to take the second highest ranking at face value, so I tested it directly. I bootstrapped a pairwise comparison, sampling the difference in ratio between Italy and each of the other 45 countries, and applied a Bonferroni correction for testing that many pairs at once. If a country's 95% interval of differences spans zero, it isn't significantly different from Italy in this two tailed test.

The grey x's mark the countries that aren't significantly different from Italy, shown in black: eleven in total, including Australia itself. Even the number one and number two spots in Hoffmann's ranking can't be reliably told apart with this data.

Given that, I don't think you can confidently claim Italy has the second highest index. Part of the problem is sample size: this was an opt in survey of baristas who watch Hoffmann's channel, not a random sample, so the number of responses per country tracks how many baristas from that country happened to answer, not anything about the country itself. Italy has about 15 responses. The USA and UK have roughly 600 each. That's nowhere near enough to pin down a precise ranking.

entry.title: Modelling Irish Hospital Trolley Counts
entry.content:
TLDR:

  • We fit a Bayesian time series model to scraped Irish hospital trolley counts, weekly for each of the six HSE regions from 2023 to 2026, scaled per 10,000 population.
  • Found a west to east pattern. The three western regions sit above the three Dublin regions, and Mid West runs at more than three times Dublin and North East.
  • Found an annual cycle, with most regions peaking in winter and Mid West's timing uncertain.
  • Found a one off drop in Mid West in August 2024 when it paused scheduled care, and given only its timing the model estimated the size of the drop and the recovery from the data.
  • The interactive results are at hsereport.ie.

Ireland's Health Service Executive (HSE) publishes a daily count of patients on hospital trolleys, people admitted through emergency departments who don't have a bed and end up being treated in a corridor or overflow ward instead. It's the number Irish news uses to talk about overcrowding. The problem is it's always reported as a raw count, and a raw count is just correlated with the region's population. We wanted to know whether, once you control for population, some parts of the country are actually under more strain than others, or whether the differences you see in the news are just noise.

We scraped the HSE's daily report every day from January 2023 to April 2026, and aggregated counts up to weekly totals for each of Ireland's six health regions. The raw weekly series below already shows a lot going on.


In the plot above, every region has a sharp dip right around New Year, marked in light blue, that lines up with hospitals discharging people over Christmas to clear beds for the January respiratory surge. And there's one dip that only shows up in a single region, HSE Mid West, in light red, in August 2024. That one turned out to be real. Mid West had paused scheduled care that month to deal with an overcrowding crisis, and it shows up cleanly in the data as an isolated drop no other region has. We call this the Mid West reset.

To compare regions properly, we built a Bayesian time series model in JAGS, with a region specific level, a region specific annual cycle, a shared New Year effect, that one off Mid West reset term, and an AR(2) term to soak up week to week persistence. Everything is scaled per 10,000 population so a region isn't penalized just for being big.

The annual cycle term is the most interesting result of all this for me. Research on Irish hospital admissions has found about a 40% increase in respiratory admissions in winter compared to summer. To investigate this in our own data, we modeled the timing of that peak for each region. Most regions do peak in winter, matching that pattern. Mid West is the exception, where the timing is uncertain. Below is the modeled peak timing by region, with winter, December through February, shaded in blue.

Another key result is what the regional levels look like once you do that, mapped below.


There's a west to east pattern in the map above that holds up statistically too. HSE Mid West runs at 8.13 trolleys per 10,000 population, more than three times HSE Dublin and North East's 2.27, and fourteen of the fifteen pairwise regional comparisons are statistically significant. The three western regions all sit above the three Dublin regions. None of this is visible in the raw totals, where a big population can make a region look worse than it actually is. This is only clear once you standardize on population, which is exactly the point of doing this properly instead of trusting the headline number.

Another interesting part was watching the model recover the shape and size of the Mid West reset. We told it which weeks were affected, since that's public record, but the size of the drop and its recovery came entirely from the data.


In the plot above, the effect bottoms out the week of August 19th at 7.29 fewer trolleys per 10,000 than the regional level, with a 95% interval that excludes zero, then rebounds back to the regional level by early September. That's a specific, dated hospital management intervention, with its magnitude inferred purely from how one region's data diverged from the rest.

As a sensitivity analysis, we checked the whole ranking against three other ways of scaling the data (per available bed, per euro of regional budget, per over 65 resident), and the top and bottom of the ranking hold up every time. Only the two middle regions swap places depending on scaling, which is a pretty reassuring sign the west to east story isn't an artifact of the specific denominator we picked.

A future direction I would like to try is adding a decision science component, putting a loss function on the posterior so the model could be used to decide where to direct resources rather than only to rank regions.

Code and data pipeline are on GitHub, and there's an interactive version of the results at hsereport.ie.

entry.title: Focaccia Recipe
entry.content:
Ingredients #

Dough:

  • 2 cups flour (Substituting 1 cup for rye or whole wheat will work fine, and lead to a hardier dough)
  • 1 teaspoon salt
  • 1 teaspoon brown sugar
  • 1.5 teaspoon instant yeast
  • `1 cup warm water
  • 1 teaspoon extra virgin olive oil (EVOO)
    Toppings:
  • chopped olives
  • chopped garlic
  • rosemary
  • EVOO

Directions #

  1. Heat up water to room temperature
  2. Mix in sugar, and yeast. Let rest.
  3. In a large bowl, whisk together your flour and salt.
  4. In a small bowl, combine chopped olives, garlic, rosemary and a few tablespoons of EVOO. Let rest.
  5. Combine the sugar-yeast-water and one tablespoon of EVOO with the dry ingredients and mix together with a spatula until fully combined. The dough should be very wet. I like to describe it as halfway between pancake batter and a country loaf.
  6. Pinch and stretch the dough up and fold it onto itself. Do this ~5 times, or until you are satisfied with yourself.
  7. Wait 5 minutes, then repeat the previous step >2 times.
  8. Let dough rest, covered in a damp towel until doubled in size. Around 1 hour if warm. Up to 3 if cold.
  9. Place into an oiled baking pan, I prefer a cast iron skillet.
  10. Preheat your oven to 450°F, 230°C. Let dough rest when oven is preheating. Be conservative with this step. Overproving can lead to denser dough.
  11. Oil your fingers and press, fingers spread, all the way into the dough until your finger tips touch the metal underneath. Do this until there are dimples roughly every 2cm.
  12. Spread topping mixture. I find it nice when an olive is stuck in the dimples.
  13. Cook for 20 minutes, or until lightly browned. Pour boiling water in a receptacle in the oven for a crispier crust.
  14. Place on cooling rack until eating temperature.

entry.title: Galette Recipe
entry.content:
*Personalized version of this recipe

Ingredients #

Topping:

  • A topping ( Enough to fill the top, extras wont hurt, I have tried strawberry, rhubarb, and apples with great success )
  • Enough sugar to coat topping in bowl

Dough:

  • 160g all-purpose flour
  • 12 g sugar
  • 1/4 teaspoon salt
  • 115g cubed unsalted butter at fridge temp
  • 70 g ice water

Frangipane:

  • 55g almond flour
  • 30 g sugar
  • 1/4 teaspoon salt
  • 30 g butter at room temperature
  • 1 egg
  • 2 teaspoons vanilla
  • Orange zest + splash of juice ( Optional )

Instructions

  1. Evenly slice the topping and put it in a bowl with sugar to breakdown. ( May produce liquid that you can withhold at the end )
  2. Heat the oven to 400ºF.
  3. To make the crust. In a food processor, pulse flour, sugar and salt together.
  4. Add the cold, cubed butter to the food processor.
  5. Pulse until the butter is the size of peas. Add ice water and pulse again until the mixture is crumbly.
  6. Lay a clean towel or cling wrap on a work surface, then dump the dough mixture into the center.
  7. Grab the opposite corners of the wrap together and twist to compress the mixture, pressing the air out and forming into a ball.
  8. Put dough ball in fridge.
  9. No need to wash food processor.
  10. For the frangipane. Combine almond flour, sugar, salt, butter, egg, and vanilla in the food processor. Mix until smooth.
  11. Lightly flour a work surface, roll out the dough into a 12+ inch circle, dusting flour when needed to prevent sticking. Transfer dough to a silicone pad for cooking, or parchment paper if you don't have.
  12. Spread the frangipane into the center leaving a 3+ cm border.
  13. Arrange your topping in an aesthetic pattern on top.
  14. Fold excess dough over to make a nice package.
  15. Brush exposed dough with egg wash mixed with a little dairy ( half and half or milk ).
  16. Sprinkle a little brown sugar on top of exposed dough. Add little knobs of button on the topping.
  17. Bake for 35 minutes or until golden brown.

entry.title: Personal Text Analysis
entry.content:
At the beginning of the year I went through a breakup and did an exploratory data analysis (EDA) of my text messages with this person.

I was interested in exploring the following questions:

What illustrative trends can we see to validate that this is normal data?
Are there observable trends in our messages leading up to the breakup?

To answer 1. I plotted the time in day that the texts take place, binned by hour. It shows what you would expect, texts drop in the middle of the night. One interesting trend is that I (orange) text a little more in the morning, and my ex (blue) is more active in the evening. Which is cool to see because I was more of a morning person.

This illustrative plot shows that my data is relatively normal, which is good because this analysis may be able to be applied to future data.

To answer 2. I applied a sentiment analysis algorithm to each text to get the table of positive or negative values for our data. I binned these values by day for each of us, and plotted them. I noticed an increased variability leading up to the breakup (which took place at the far right of the plot).

The next plot is of the variance, binned by week this time, to capture the day to day variability seen in the prior plot.

As my ex and I were working through our issues, we would have days where we feel like we are going to make it, followed up by days where we both feel like it's over. The intense switching of positive and negative emotions can be seen in this data! This was so cool for me to see and is one of the reasons I love data analysis of contemporary issues. You can observe trends that you feel!

I do have one lingering question. Do these trends express themselves in other breakups? I scoured the internet and unfortunately could not find any ethical data.

This was a cool project for me and I hope someone could get some value out of it too. :)
